identity.title: The Kinematics of z ≳ 6 Quasar Host Galaxies

paper_type_evidence.quote: We explore the kinematics of 27 $z \gtrsim 6$ quasar host galaxies observed in \[C II\]-158$\mu$m (\[C II\]) emission with the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array at a resolution of $\approx$ $0.25\ensuremath{''}$.

We have therefore obtained $<$$0.25\ensuremath{''}$ (which is $<$1.2 kpc at $z \approx 6$) \[C II\] imaging of $z \gtrsim 6$ quasar host galaxies using ALMA over several observing programs (in particular recent program IDs: 2017.1.01301.S and 2018.1.00908.S).

question.value: What are the kinematic properties, dynamical masses, gas mass fractions, and positions relative to the local black hole-bulge mass relation of 27 z >= 6 quasar host galaxies resolved in [C II] emission?

evidence.quote: We explore the kinematics of 27 $z \gtrsim 6$ quasar host galaxies observed in \[C II\]-158$\mu$m (\[C II\]) emission with the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array at a resolution of $\approx$ $0.25\ensuremath{''}$.

This allows us to determine if quasars preferentially occur in galaxies with certain kinematic properties or shows hints of recent mergers, as well as provide some of the most reliable estimates for the dynamical mass of any sample of $z \gtrsim 6$ quasar host galaxies.

findings_qualitative.value: Roughly one-third (9/27) of z >= 6 quasar host galaxies have disturbed [C II] morphologies due to companions or mergers, one-third (10/27) show smooth velocity gradients consistent with rotating disks, and one-third (8/27) lack velocity gradients and appear dispersion-dominated.

findings_qualitative.value: The z ~ 2 main-sequence [C II]-to-molecular gas conversion factor (alpha_[CII] = 31 L_sun/M_sun) overpredicts molecular gas masses above the dynamical masses at z >= 6 and is therefore likely invalid for z >= 6 quasar hosts.

evidence.quote: We find that if we apply the molecular mass conversion from the \[C II\] luminosity assuming the conversion in (cite: Zanella2018), we get molecular mass estimates that are on-average greater than the dynamical mass estimates with a median molecular-to-dynamical mass ratio of 1.7.
This suggests that the conversion factor derived for main-sequence galaxies at $z \sim 2$ is not valid for quasar host galaxies at $z \gtrsim 6$.

findings_qualitative.value: The diversity of [C II] kinematics (mergers, rotating disks, turbulent dispersion-dominated systems) suggests that gas accretion onto z >= 6 SMBHs is not triggered by a single precipitating factor.

evidence.quote: Finally, we speculate that the large variety in \[C II\] kinematics is an indication that gas accretion onto $z \gtrsim 6$ super massive black holes is not caused by a single precipitating factor.

claims.hypothesis: Luminous z >= 6 quasars are primarily triggered by a single mechanism (such as major mergers) and therefore share uniform host galaxy kinematics.
claims.experiment: Morphological and 3D kinematic analysis of [C II] 158 um emission at ~0.25'' resolution across 27 z >= 6 quasar host galaxies using qubefit and 2D Gaussian spectral fitting.
claims.result: 9 of 27 galaxies show disturbed/merger [C II] emission, 10 of 27 show smooth velocity gradients consistent with rotating disks, and 8 of 27 show no velocity gradient and higher velocity dispersions (153 +/- 32 km s^-1 vs 95 +/- 25 km s^-1).
claims.finding: Gas accretion onto z >= 6 SMBHs is not caused by a single precipitating factor; quasar hosts exhibit diverse kinematic states.

evidence.quote: We find that nine of the galaxies show disturbed \[C II\] emission, either due to a close companion galaxy or recent merger. Ten galaxies have smooth velocity gradients consistent with the emission arising from a gaseous disk. The remaining eight quasar host galaxies show no velocity gradient, suggesting that the gas in these systems is dispersion-dominated.
Finally, we speculate that the large variety in \[C II\] kinematics is an indication that gas accretion onto $z \gtrsim 6$ super massive black holes is not caused by a single precipitating factor.

claims.hypothesis: The high velocity dispersions of z >= 6 quasar host galaxies follow the general cosmological redshift evolution of galaxy turbulence rather than requiring AGN-driven elevation.
claims.experiment: Measure beam-smearing-corrected velocity dispersions for the undisturbed quasar host sample with qubefit and compare against an exponential extrapolation of z <= 4 galaxy samples.
claims.result: The undisturbed sample has a mean velocity dispersion of 129 +/- 10 km s^-1 (median 123 km s^-1), which lies on the exponential extrapolation of lower-redshift measurements.
claims.finding: The high velocity dispersions can be explained by the higher redshift of the sample without requiring additional dispersion from the central AGN, though sample selection differences remain a caveat.

evidence.quote: The mean velocity dispersion for the undisturbed sample is $129 \pm 10$ km s$^{-1}$.
Extrapolating an exponential fit to this evolution out to $z \gtrsim 6$ shows that the quasar population falls on this extrapolation (Figure 5).

claims.hypothesis: z >= 6 quasar host galaxies lie on the local bulge mass - black hole mass relation.
claims.experiment: Derive dynamical masses within 2 R_e from 3D [C II] kinematic modeling (accounting for disk potential, pressure support eta, and radius systematics) and compare with literature SMBH masses and the local Kormendy & Ho (2013) relation.
claims.result: The undisturbed sample has a mean dynamical mass of 5.0 +/- 0.8 (+/- 3.5) x 10^10 M_sun, which is about a factor of seven smaller than local counterparts at the same SMBH mass (a 2.4 sigma deviation above the local relation).
claims.finding: z >= 6 quasar host galaxies are less massive than expected from the local M_bulge - M_BH relation at 2.4 sigma significance, unless dynamical mass systematically underestimates stellar bulge mass.

evidence.quote: This results in a mean dynamical mass of $5.0\,\pm\,0.8\,(\pm\,3.5) \times 10^{10} M_\odot$. Comparison between the dynamical mass and the mass of the supermassive black hole reveals that the sample falls above the locally derived bulge mass–black hole mass relation at 2.4$\sigma$ significance.

evidence.loc: Comparison between Dynamical and SMBH Mass
evidence.quote: Comparing the mean of the $z \gtrsim 6$ quasar sample, in which the uncertainties are dominated by the systematics described in the previous sections, with the local relationship of (cite: Kormendy2013) shows that the dynamical masses of these quasars are smaller by about a factor of seven, which is a 2.4$\sigma$ deviation from the local correlation.

claims.hypothesis: Molecular gas constitutes a large fraction (>10%) of the total dynamical mass within the inner few kpc of z >= 6 quasar host galaxies.
claims.experiment: Estimate molecular gas masses from far-infrared dust continuum and from [C II] luminosity, and compare against dynamical masses within 2 R_e.
claims.result: Dust continuum yields a median M_gas / M_dyn ratio of 0.3 (and >10% even after accounting for spatial extent and dust temperature/beta uncertainties), while the z ~ 2 [C II] conversion yields a median ratio of 1.7.
claims.finding: Molecular gas makes up >10% of the dynamical mass (and a large fraction of the baryonic mass) in z >= 6 quasar host galaxies, while the z ~ 2 [C II]-to-M_gas conversion overestimates gas mass at z >= 6.

evidence.quote: Using several different estimators for the molecular mass, we estimate a gas mass fraction of $>$10 %, indicating gas makes up a large fraction of the baryonic mass of $z \gtrsim 6$ quasar host galaxies.
When we use the dust continuum emission to estimate the molecular mass, we find a molecular-to-dynamical mass ratio of 0.3.

why_this_data.value: Sub-0.25'' (<1.2 kpc at z ~ 6) ALMA [C II] observations are required to spatially resolve the ~0.4'' (~2 kpc) extent of z >= 6 quasar host galaxies, overcome optical/NIR quasar glare, and constrain morphology, inclination, and kinematics.

evidence.quote: Unlike the optical and near-infrared, where the brightness of the quasar inhibits detection of the quasar host galaxy, the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) capitalizes on the relative faintness of the quasar at millimeter wavelengths in order to search for the quasar host.

Previous observations have shown that the extent of the \[C II\] emission from these galaxies is $\approx$$0.4\ensuremath{''}$ corresponding to $\approx$2 kpc (cite: Walter2009; Wang2013; Venemans2016; Decarli2018). We have therefore obtained $<$$0.25\ensuremath{''}$ (which is $<$1.2 kpc at $z \approx 6$) \[C II\] imaging of $z \gtrsim 6$ quasar host galaxies using ALMA over several observing programs (in particular recent program IDs: 2017.1.01301.S and 2018.1.00908.S).

why_this_method.value: Direct 3D cube forward modeling with qubefit accounts for finite beam resolution/smearing and allows flexible non-disk models, while spaxel-by-spaxel 1D Gaussian fitting avoids the clipping artifacts that bias moment-based velocity dispersion maps at low S/N.

evidence.quote: In order to capture the increasing complexity of far-infrared emission line observations, and to allow for maximum flexibility in emission models, we have designed the Python-based code `qubefit`.

evidence.loc: Two Methods for Deriving Mean Velocity and Velocity Dispersion Fields
evidence.quote: Because of the robust nature of the Gaussian fitting and its independence on the noise properties of the data, we opt to use this method for estimating the velocity and velocity dispersion fields for all quasar host galaxies in our sample.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: 2D moment 1 and moment 2 maps with sigma-clipping were tested and rejected for deriving velocity and dispersion fields because clipping at >= 2 sigma artificially lowers the velocity dispersion at the low-S/N edges of the galaxy.

evidence.loc: Two Methods for Deriving Mean Velocity and Velocity Dispersion Fields
evidence.quote: Aggressive clipping can therefore significantly alter the velocity dispersion field, resulting in low S/N regions having artificially low velocity dispersions.

evidence.loc: Two Methods for Deriving Mean Velocity and Velocity Dispersion Fields
evidence.quote: Because of the robust nature of the Gaussian fitting and its independence on the noise properties of the data, we opt to use this method for estimating the velocity and velocity dispersion fields for all quasar host galaxies in our sample.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: More complicated emission profiles (e.g., double exponential) and radial velocity/dispersion profiles were tested in qubefit, but rejected because they did not improve the fit or change conclusions at ~0.25'' resolution.

evidence.quote: Although in (cite: Novak2020) we find that the \[C II\] emission is best described by a compact and extended component, introducing a more complicated emission profile does not improve the fit.
We have tested more complicated velocity and dispersion profiles, but these do not change our conclusions.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Dispersion-dominated spherical bulge model was fit to all galaxies, but provided a poorer fit than the thin disk model for systems with rotation or asymmetric morphologies, so the thin disk model was used for subsequent analysis.

evidence.quote: In general, the dispersion-dominated bulge model provides a poorer fit to the data than the thin disk model.
For the remainder of the paper, we will therefore use the results from the thin disk model.

limitations_admitted.value: Convolving the model with a frequency-independent 2D Gaussian beam on a small region of the cleaned cube and using a scalar f_beam factor are approximations to the true dirty beam and pixel-to-pixel covariance matrix.

evidence.quote: We note that this is an approximation in two ways: 1) The actual beam (often referred to as the ‘dirty’ beam) is much more complicated in interferometric data, hence the need for removing the beam before analyzing the data in a process known as *cleaning*.

We note that this is an approximation to the true correlated nature of the observations, which requires accounting for the covariance matrix describing the pixel-to-pixel correlations as well as the uncertainty in the $\chi^2$ statistic (cite: Davis2017; Smith2019).

limitations_admitted.value: Four undisturbed galaxies (J0842+1218, J1044-0125, J2100-1715, J2348-3054) are only barely resolved and one (P323+12) is detected at very low significance, making kinematic modeling and inclination constraints difficult.

evidence.quote: We note that the \[C II\] emission from four of these galaxies (see Table 1) is only barely resolved, and one quasar host galaxy (P323$+$12) is only detected at very low significance.

However, some of the quasar host galaxies are only barely resolved in these observations, and have large uncertainties on the inclination of the \[C II\] emission (i.e., J0842$+$1218, J1044$-$0125, J2100$-$1715, P323$+$12 and J2348$-$3054).

limitations_admitted.value: The ~0.25'' spatial resolution is insufficient to resolve the rising part of the rotation curve (which requires at least 4 beams along the major axis) or the SMBH sphere of influence.

evidence.loc: Radial Profiles of the Mean Velocity and Velocity Dispersion
evidence.quote: The resolution of these observations is therefore insufficient to measure the shape of the rotation curve, which requires at least four independent measurements along the major axis.

evidence.loc: Radial Profiles of the Mean Velocity and Velocity Dispersion
evidence.quote: We note in passing here that the current resolution remains too coarse to resolve the SMBH’s sphere of influence.

limitations_admitted.value: For galaxies in the disturbed/merger subsample, the assumption of gravitationally supported motion in a single smooth disk breaks down and yields unreliable inclinations and dynamical masses.

evidence.quote: In some cases (i.e., J1342$+$0928, P308$-$21 and J2318$-$3113), the model tries to fit multiple distinct \[C II\] components with a single smooth disk. This causes unreasonably large inclinations (the median inclination is about 20$\ensuremath{^\circ}$ larger) in the merger subsample, and hence results in inaccurate kinematic parameters for these galaxies.

We measure the dynamical masses for all galaxies in the sample, although we caution that the estimates for galaxies in the disturbed sample are not very reliable due to non-gravitationally supported motions.

limitations_admitted.value: Equating [C II] dynamical mass to stellar bulge mass carries large systematic uncertainties that could alleviate the 2.4 sigma offset from the local M_bulge - M_BH relation.

evidence.loc: Comparison between Dynamical and SMBH Mass
evidence.quote: A detailed discussion on the magnitude of this systematic is beyond the scope of this work, but if the results from NGC 3091 are typical, then much of the tension between high redshift quasars and the local bulge mass - black hole mass relation could be alleviated by accounting for this systematic.

referee_caveats_inferred: The inclination angles for several low-inclination or barely resolved disks have only upper limits, resulting in only lower limits on v_rot and M_dyn for 5 of the 18 undisturbed sources.
Using a single isotropic pressure-support factor eta = 3.4 for both rotation-dominated and dispersion-dominated systems introduces substantial systematic uncertainty in circular velocity.

code_released.value: qubefit is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/mneeleman/qubefit

evidence.quote: To provide an estimate of the dynamical mass within twice the half-light radius of the quasar host galaxy, we model the kinematics of the \[C II\] emission line using our publicly available kinematic fitting code, `qubefit`.
https://github.com/mneeleman/qubefit

Appendix C defines the 9-parameter thin disk kinematic model used in qubefit
Turbulent pressure-supported exponential disk formalism used to set eta = 3.4 in circular velocity calculation
Methodology and comparison for deriving 2D velocity fields via Gaussian profile fitting vs moments
Methodology for converting far-infrared dust continuum flux density into dust and molecular gas mass
Conversion factor alpha_[CII] = 31 L_sun/M_sun between [C II] luminosity and molecular gas mass
